To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) the prevalence of malicious activity in crowdsourced surveys is high, and (b) the prevalence of untrustworthy workers is higher than the prevalence of malicious workers.
(1) the most common form of malicious behavior is spamming, which is followed by cheating, and (2) there exist different types of workers, which exhibit different behavioral patterns.

the prevalence of malicious behavior on crowdsourcing platforms is high; the most common types of malicious behavior are cheating, shilling, and spamming; the most prevalent malicious activity on online surveys is cheating; the prevalence of cheating on online surveys is 20%; and the most common types among the cheating workers are the “cheater” and “cheating spammer” types.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of surveys that are resilient to malicious behavior and are capable of eliciting truthful responses from the workers.
understanding the behavior of workers on crowdsourcing platforms, with an aim to design better quality control mechanisms and improve the efficiency of crowdsourcing tasks.
the design and implementation of quality control mechanisms that are effective against malicious behavior on crowdsourcing platforms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the crowdsourcing platform is an ideal place for the malicious workers to exploit the system.
we need to understand the behavior of the crowd to prevent exploitation of tasks and ensure the quality of results produced.
the crowd is not as bad as it is made out to be, and the majority of workers can be relied upon to complete tasks with integrity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the behavior exhibited by workers in the crowd can be classified into four distinct categories: honest workers, cheaters, spammers, and malicious workers.
we have identified and characterized different types of workers and their behavior, and proposed a mechanism to detect malicious behavior in crowdsourced surveys.
we present an understanding of the prevalent malicious activity in crowdsourcing platforms and provide insights on how to design surveys in order to minimize malicious behavior.
The main takeaway from our work is that
malicious activity on crowdsourced surveys can be detected and prevented with the help of a simple set of design guidelines.
the design of crowdsourced tasks should be based on an in-depth understanding of the behavior of workers in the crowds.
malicious activity on crowdsourced surveys can be effectively mitigated if the survey designer understands the behavior of workers and the nature of the task at hand.
